findings.title: Exposed .env file (secrets served from web root)
findings.why_it_matters: Your .env — database URLs, API keys, JWT secrets — is downloadable by anyone.
findings.remediation: Stop serving dotfiles from the web root, move secrets out of the served directory, and ROTATE every key that was exposed.

findings.title: Exposed SQL database dump (backup.sql)
findings.why_it_matters: /backup.sql is downloadable by anyone — a database dump or config backup hands over your data and secrets wholesale.
findings.remediation: Remove backup/dump files from the web root and block dotfile/backup extensions at the web server; rotate anything exposed.

findings.title: Stripe secret key exposed in client code
findings.why_it_matters: A Stripe SECRET key is shipped to the browser — anyone who views source can charge cards and issue refunds on your account.
findings.remediation: Move the secret key server-side, use only the publishable key client-side, and rotate the exposed key now.

findings.title: AWS access key id exposed in client code
findings.why_it_matters: An AWS access key id is embedded in client code — a path to full cloud-account abuse if the secret is nearby or reused.
findings.remediation: Remove AWS credentials from the frontend and rotate the key immediately.

findings.title: Guessable password-reset token on /password-reset
findings.why_it_matters: The reset token is only 9 characters (low entropy, brute-forceable), so an attacker can guess it outright. A leaked or guessable reset token is full account takeover — the single most damaging bug a vibe-coded auth flow ships with.
findings.remediation: Never return the reset token in the API response — email a link to the registered address only. Use a cryptographically random token (>=32 chars), single-use, short-lived, and rate-limit the reset endpoint.

findings.title: Password-reset token exposed in the response on /api/password/forgot
findings.why_it_matters: The reset token is returned in the HTTP response instead of being emailed, so anyone who can call this endpoint can take over the account. A leaked or guessable reset token is full account takeover — the single most damaging bug a vibe-coded auth flow ships with.
findings.remediation: Never return the reset token in the API response — email a link to the registered address only. Use a cryptographically random token (>=32 chars), single-use, short-lived, and rate-limit the reset endpoint.

findings.title: Cross-account object read (IDOR/BOLA) on /api/invoices/{id}
findings.why_it_matters: Two different logged-in users (alice and bob) receive the same private object at /api/invoices/117. The endpoint never checks ownership, so any authenticated user can read anyone else's records.
findings.remediation: Enforce an ownership/authorization check (object.owner_id == the current user) before returning the object; return 403 otherwise.

findings.title: CORS reflects any origin with credentials on /api/me
findings.why_it_matters: The endpoint echoes any website's Origin and allows credentials, so a malicious site can read this authenticated response from a logged-in user's browser.
findings.remediation: Never reflect the Origin header. Allow only an explicit allowlist of trusted origins, and don't combine a wildcard origin with credentials.

findings.title: Reflected input (likely XSS) via ?q= on /search
findings.why_it_matters: The `q` parameter is reflected into the HTML response unencoded, so an attacker can inject script and run it in a victim's browser (reflected XSS).
findings.remediation: Context-encode all user input on output (HTML-escape), and add a Content-Security-Policy as defense in depth.

findings.title: Stack trace / debug output leaked on /api/calc
findings.why_it_matters: The app returns internal stack traces or debug pages to clients, exposing file paths, framework internals and sometimes secrets — and it usually means debug mode is enabled in production.
findings.remediation: Turn off debug mode in production and return generic error pages; log the details server-side only.

findings.title: Missing security headers (x-content-type-options, x-frame-options, content-security-policy, referrer-policy)
findings.why_it_matters: Without these headers the app is exposed in the browser to MIME-type sniffing, clickjacking, cross-site scripting and content injection, leaking URLs to third parties via the Referer header — cheap, high-value hardening a vibe-coded app almost always skips.
findings.remediation: Send `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`. Send `X-Frame-Options: DENY` (or a CSP `frame-ancestors 'none'`). Add a restrictive `Content-Security-Policy`, e.g. `default-src 'self'`. Send `Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin`.

findings.title: Session cookie 'session' set without HttpOnly
findings.why_it_matters: The 'session' cookie is readable from JavaScript, so any XSS on the site can steal the session and impersonate the user.
findings.remediation: Set the cookie with HttpOnly (and Secure + SameSite): e.g. `Set-Cookie: session=...; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax`.

findings.title: Open redirect via ?url= on /redirect
findings.why_it_matters: The `url` parameter sends users to any URL, so an attacker can craft a link on your domain that lands victims on a phishing site.
findings.remediation: Redirect only to a known allowlist of internal paths, or validate the target is same-origin before redirecting.

findings.title: GraphQL introspection enabled on /graphql
findings.why_it_matters: Introspection is on, so anyone can download your full GraphQL schema — every type, field and mutation — making the rest of the API trivial to attack.
findings.remediation: Disable introspection in production (e.g. the GraphQL server's introspection flag), or gate it behind authentication.

findings.title: Prometheus metrics endpoint exposed
findings.why_it_matters: Operational metrics (and often internal hostnames and counts) are public.
findings.remediation: Require authentication for /metrics or bind it to an internal network only.

findings.title: Open directory listing at /files/
findings.why_it_matters: Anyone can browse every file under /files/ — including backups, dumps and source that were never meant to be downloadable.
findings.remediation: Turn off directory autoindex (e.g. nginx `autoindex off`) and serve an explicit index or 403 instead.

findings.title: Exposed docker-compose.yml
findings.why_it_matters: /docker-compose.yml is downloadable, exposing your service layout, image/registry names and pipeline — and sometimes embedded secrets.
findings.remediation: Don't deploy CI/infra config to the web root; block these filenames at the web server.

findings.title: Host header reflected on /password-reset
findings.why_it_matters: The app trusts the Host header to build absolute links, so an attacker can set Host to their domain and poison password-reset links or caches.
findings.remediation: Build absolute URLs from a configured canonical host, not the request Host header; validate Host against an allowlist.

findings.title: Technology disclosed via X-Powered-By (Express)
findings.why_it_matters: The X-Powered-By header advertises 'Express', telling an attacker which framework to target — free reconnaissance you can remove. (Informational.)
findings.remediation: Remove the X-Powered-By header (e.g. Express: `app.disable('x-powered-by')`) and suppress versioned Server banners.
